source.title: Understanding Generalization in Deep Learning via Tensor Methods
source.authors: Jingling Li; Yanchao Sun; Jia-Hao Su; Taiji Suzuki; Furong Huang

record.tranche_reason: Tests how a tensor-factorized CNN architecture affects test performance under clean and corrupted-label training, using standard CNNs as comparators. It does not directly test any listed version.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training and test accuracy for CP-layer and standard CNNs, plus test accuracy under label corruption. Its measured weight properties and generalization bounds also relate to generalization, but the specific bound/property values are not themselves train–test gap results. Cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates tensor-based compression bounds and CP-layer architectures, but tests none of V1–V8. Partial label corruption with evaluation on clean test labels does not establish V1's coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label generalization. Its compression measures do not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors claim useful tensor-based compression bounds, improved compressibility, and improved robustness and generalization under label noise. They describe clean-label accuracy as competitive, not improved. The record's claimed clean-accuracy advantage reverses Table 1's column headings.
record.recipe_differences: Uses standard SGD with momentum, weight decay, and scheduled learning rates, while changing the architecture to include CP layers; evaluates label corruption but does not conduct the fixed-random-label comparison in V1.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported architecture advantage under label corruption varies with corruption rate; the authors say improvement has low effect at Symmetric-20% corruption.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 1 reports 100% training accuracy for all four models. Its with-CPL columns have lower clean CIFAR10 test accuracy: 93.68% versus 95.09% for VGG-16, and 92.64% versus the externally reported 95.83% for WRN-28-10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: CP-layer networks retain competitive clean-label classification accuracy, although Table 1 does not show a clean-accuracy improvement over standard networks.

fits_no_version.finding: On CIFAR10, CP-VGG-16 exceeds VGG-16 test accuracy at corruption rates 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8: 71.09 versus 68.76, 51.76 versus 44.26, 35.60 versus 24.89, and 20.06 versus 13.21 percent. The supplied table preserves these mappings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: CP layers improve clean-test accuracy after training on partially corrupted labels in the tested VGG-16 settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 2b shows the proposed compression bound following test-error changes during CP-VGG-16 training; Figures 3 and 8 compare compression properties under clean and corrupted training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tensor-based compressibility measures can characterize generalization in the studied networks.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS 2020)
record.problems: Table 2 is flattened in the supplied text and does not securely preserve the mapping of all values to conditions. Clean-accuracy results have no reported uncertainty. The label-corruption evidence does not test fitting fully random labels or held-out performance on random labels.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Property plots and bound comparisons are not train–test gap outcomes for the listed versions; the supplied text gives some results only as figures without recoverable numeric values.

untested.parts: No fully randomized-label fitting result or corresponding chance-level held-out result is reported. Clean accuracy and partially corrupted-label test accuracy do not establish the conjunction; training also uses weight decay.
No width sweep beyond the width required for zero training error. Figure 5 varies CP compression ratios under co-teaching without establishing an interpolation threshold.
No empirical convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison or isolation of local connectivity.
No batch-size comparison under fixed or adapted training budgets.
Dropout is absent rather than experimentally varied.
No magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness measurement or ranking of generalization gaps against norm and margin measures.
No removal of examples selected by memorization influence followed by retraining and comparison with random removal.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because their measures do not establish those versions; this does not mean Table 2's values are unreadable. No verdict labels apply.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report fitting fully randomized training labels and evaluating held-out accuracy on those same randomized labels against chance.
No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
Does not compare convolutional networks with fully connected networks or isolate local connectivity.
All described experiments use no dropout; dropout is not varied.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare sharpness measures as predictors of the train–test gap.
Does not remove memorized examples and retrain.

rows.subject: VGG-16
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR10 with standard optimization settings and no dropout; clean-label accuracy reported.
rows.check: Table 1 places 'with CPL' before 'without CPL'. For standard VGG-16, the CIFAR10 values are training 100%, test 95.09%, rather than 93.68%. Neither outcome tests a listed version.

rows.subject: CP-VGG-16
rows.size_stated: same number of parameters as VGG-16
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR10 with CP layers and standard optimization settings; clean-label accuracy reported.
rows.note: The authors describe training and test accuracy as competitive; CP-VGG-16 test accuracy is higher in this table.
rows.check: CP-VGG-16 has training 100%, test 93.68%; its standard VGG-16 comparator has test 95.09%. The record reverses the columns and the direction of the comparison. This is the study's proposed architecture performance, outside the listed versions.

rows.subject: WRN-28-10

rows.check: Standard WRN-28-10 has test accuracy 95.83%, rather than 92.64%. The 95.83% entry is starred and attributed to Zagoruyko and Komodakis (2016), so it should be identified as an externally reported comparator rather than this study's own training result.
